body:
Parent: [#6018](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/6018) (Atlas ingestion program). Statements S16–S20, S29, S30 of the 2026-11-04 brief.

## Requirement (Drew, in substance)

Atlas must understand **content versioning** well enough that:

1. **New versions of files are first-class**: a changed file lands as a new version of the same object, never an overwrite and never an unrelated new object.
2. **Renames are understood**: a renamed file's versions continue the same lineage. For git sources this is simple **if commits are done in the right way** (renames recorded as renames instead of delete+insert) — the design may set commit-hygiene expectations for source repos, and must handle non-git sources (session stores, doc trees) where lineage has to be inferred (segment association, sibling design under [#3125](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/3125)).
3. **Old and new are both kept**, but resolution defaults to **"the max" — the newest version of every file**. Search/retrieval asks for a file and gets its latest version unless it explicitly addresses history.
4. **Old versions roll out to cold storage** over time (2026-11-04 storage ruling: cold tiers → rustfs) — a lifecycle with hot → cold movement, not permanent hot residence.
5. **Old versions are eventually removed** under an explicit policy with three named triggers, any of which can retire a version:
   - **by date** — older than a threshold;
   - **by increments** — N newer versions exist beyond it;
   - **by access** — it has never (or no longer) been retrieved (this trigger consumes the retrieval statistics from the sibling stats/feedback design under [#6018](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/6018)).

## Tensions the design must face honestly

- [#3125](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/3125) carries Drew's 2026-10-31 rule: **keep ALL data; nothing stripped to save space; only byte-identical dupes cleaned**. The deletion policy above is a deliberate evolution of that rule (2026-11-04 brief) — the design must state which rule governs which tier/class, and default to keep unless a trigger AND a class rule both say retire. Deletion of a version must never orphan chunks whose occurrences point at it (occurrence registry semantics per #3125).
- Newest-resolution interacts with fan-out search ([#5755](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5755)) and the parameter surface ([#5774](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5774)): `as-of` / version pinning becomes a query parameter, and full-version logging per run must record WHICH version of each file a result came from (feeds the query-trace design).
- Cold rollout must preserve resolvability: a cold version still resolves (slower) until a deletion trigger fires; deletion is the only hard end.

## Design must answer

- The version object model: identity (file id vs version id), lineage edges (rename, edit, split/merge of files), and how chunks map to versions (shared chunks across versions recorded as occurrences, not copies).
- Per-class retention defaults (code, docs, session logs, chat logs, generated reports likely differ) and who can override them.
- The retrieval-side contract: default-latest semantics, explicit history addressing, and how merge/rescore treats multi-version hits for the same file (one file, best version, unless the query is historical).

## Done looks like

A design doc in code (`doc/`): version model, lineage rules per source type, retention policy table with the three triggers parameterized per class, cold-tier mechanics, and the query-side version contract — with implementation split into follow-ons.
